title: Code, QA and Production Agents
promise: From issue to deploy without scares: small diffs written by agents, tests that stop bad changes, PRs reviewed by humans, and a rollback you've rehearsed.
audience: anyone maintaining software in production with a small team: the technical person at an SME, the two-developer studio, the freelancer with five clients
plain: This is about putting code agents (Claude Code, Codex) to work without one of them taking down production on a Friday. The wrong idea is "the AI programs for me"; the idea that works is an assembly line with brakes: every job starts as a well-written issue (what to change, what not to touch, how it's checked), the agent works on a branch with a small diff, tests pass before anyone looks, a person reviews the PR understanding what they're approving, deploy is boring and automatic, and if something goes wrong the rollback is rehearsed and takes two minutes. Every piece exists because its absence has a name and a face: without a clear issue the agent invents scope; without a small diff, review is theater; without tests you approve blind; without a rehearsed rollback, the 6pm error lasts until 11pm. The result isn't coding without knowing how: it's one technical person alone performing like a small team, with the agent doing the mechanical work and the person supplying judgment. It works just as well for the company website as for the internal app or the five client projects you maintain.
fits: You maintain a website or app in production and the backlog of fixes grows faster than you can clear it
You're the only technical person around and small fixes eat the hours that matter
A small studio wanting to take on more maintenance clients without hiring yet
You use Claude Code or Codex on and off, with no method: sometimes gold, sometimes half the repo rewritten
Bugs get jotted down on WhatsApp or in your head, and get patched live on production
There are no tests and every change gets "clicked around a bit" before shipping
Deploy is a fearful ritual: shipped on Friday while praying, or not shipped for weeks
You inherited a project from another developer and need to change it without breaking it
You want to standardize how you work with agents so you can delegate or bill maintenance properly
Clients ask for small changes constantly and the back-and-forth eats your margin
notFor: Learning to code from scratch: this kit provides method on top of existing technical judgment; without someone who understands the diffs, review is theater, and theater in production is expensive
Life-or-death systems, money in transit, or medical data: the QA and audit bar there is well above what this kit builds
Full rewrites or big migrations: agents help, but that's a project with its own plan, not a chain of small issues
Code with no version control or organized deploy permissions: Git and access first, agents after
Large teams with mature engineering processes already in place: this kit will feel small on them; its value is bringing that order to teams of one to three people

scopes.label: Minimum
scopes.what: One project with an organized repository, an issue template, the agent always working on a branch with a small diff, smoke tests for the three critical routes, PRs reviewed by you, and a deploy with a rollback rehearsed once.
scopes.time: A week here and there, 10-12 hours
scopes.cost: €0-20/month: free GitHub and Vercel, the agent's subscription or API
scopes.skip: Skip the automated issue circuit and the metrics: branch discipline, small diffs, tests and review already eliminate 80% of the scares.

scopes.label: Standard
scopes.what: Everything in minimum plus CI that runs tests and linter on every PR, test coverage on the routes that move money or data, this kit's circuit (labeled issue → agent plan → approval → work), a change log per project, and deploys with post-deploy verification.
scopes.time: Three weeks here and there, about 25 hours
scopes.cost: €20-70/month: agent, CI within GitHub Actions' free tier, and tooling
scopes.skip: Skip per-project staging environments if your projects are stateless websites: Vercel previews cover most cases.

scopes.label: Advanced
scopes.what: Everything above plus several projects under the same method, staging where it's needed, production error alerts (Sentry or similar), a measured token budget per project, and the incident playbook rehearsed with a drill.
scopes.cost: €70-200/month depending on projects and agent volume
scopes.skip: Don't start here. The method gets learned on one project and copied to the others; setting it up on five at once multiplies the fronts without multiplying the learning.

brief.name: Define your chain before you turn the agent loose
brief.when: First thing. Before installing anything, before handing a repository to an agent, before promising new speeds.
brief.prompt:
Act as a technical lead experienced with one-to-three-person teams using code agents. We're going to build an issue → branch → small diff → tests → PR → deploy → rollback chain, and I want you to force me to define it against my reality, not the theory.

My context:
- Projects in production: how many, what they are, what tech: [PROJECTS]
- Who touches them and what they know: [TEAM]
- How a change gets requested today and reaches production, step by step, warts included: [PROCESS TODAY]
- The real state of the repository: are there branches? tests? CI? can you deploy with one button?: [STATE]
- The last three scares in production and what caused them: [SCARES]
- Which parts of the system move money, personal data, or affect real users: [CRITICAL]
- What agent I use or want to use and how much experience: [AGENT]
- Hours per week to set this up and to maintain it: [HOURS]

Do this, in this order:

1. Hand my current process back to me as a chain of links, marking which ones have no brake today (what stops a bad change from reaching production right now? if the answer is "nothing" or "me being careful," mark it). Mark anything you're assuming with a WARNING.
2. Ask me only the three questions that would change the design the most. Stop cold and wait.
3. When I answer, tell me what an agent must NOT touch in my case: the files, modules or decisions where the cost of a mistake exceeds what it saves. Be strict: data migrations, payments, authentication and deploy configuration usually belong on that list.
4. Propose the order to build the brakes in, starting with whichever prevents the most of my scares, with my list of scares in front of you. Don't make me build perfect CI before I have smoke tests.
5. Write the success criteria with numbers: the max diff size I'll actually review, time from issue to production for a small change, rollback time, and how many of my typical scares the chain would have stopped.

Don't recommend new tools if the ones I have work. If my case doesn't need agents (a tiny project, rare changes), tell me: the braking method still applies without them.

fill.what: What you maintain, with tech and size
fill.example: The company website (Next.js on Vercel), an internal order app (React + Supabase), and two client websites

fill.what: Who touches code and their level
fill.example: Just me; I know how to code but I'm pressed for time, plus a colleague who understands SQL
They ask me on WhatsApp, I change main directly, I test by clicking around and push. Sometimes on Fridays
Git yes, branches almost never, zero tests, Vercel auto-deploys on push

fill.what: The last three incidents, with cause
fill.example: A style change broke checkout; an updated dependency killed the build; I deleted a field another part used
The order form and a client's payment gateway

fill.what: What you work with and your comfort level
fill.example: Claude Code in the terminal, two months using it with no fixed method

fill.what: Real time to set up and maintain
fill.example: 4 hours a week for a month, then whatever it saves

brief.expect: Your current chain with the unbraked links marked, three questions, the list of what the agent doesn't touch, the build order against your real scares, and the success criteria with numbers.
brief.stuck: If it hands you back the ideal process of a twenty-person team (sprints, two approvers, triple staging), trim it: "it's just me; give me the minimal version of each brake that still brakes." The kit is proportional brakes, not bureaucracy.

architecture.what: The job written in a format an agent can't misread: what to change, what not to touch, how to check it's done.
architecture.nocode: A GitHub issue template with three required fields: change, boundaries, acceptance criteria.
architecture.code: The same template as a GitHub issue form (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE) with required fields.
architecture.why: The issue is the prompt. A vague issue produces a huge diff that touches things it shouldn't: the agent fills ambiguity with initiative, and an agent's initiative in your production is exactly what you don't want.

architecture.what: Every issue is worked on its own branch; main is always deployable.
architecture.nocode: The rule written down and main-branch protection turned on in GitHub (nobody pushes directly, not even you).
architecture.code: A branch named with the issue number, and main protected requiring PR and green checks.
architecture.why: The branch is what lets you throw a failed experiment in the trash without cleanup. With agents it matters doubly: their cheap way to fail is a deleted branch, not a revert on main.

architecture.layer: 3. The agent with context and a leash
architecture.what: Claude Code or Codex working with the project's rules in front of it and the issue's scope as the boundary.
architecture.nocode: A CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md file in the repository: architecture in ten lines, commands, what not to touch, how it's tested.
architecture.code: The same, plus per-directory instructions in larger projects.
architecture.why: The context file is the difference between explaining the project every session and it already knowing it. And a "don't touch" list inside the repository outweighs saying it in the prompt: it's always there, whoever's looking.

architecture.what: The change fits inside an honest review: as a rule, under 200 lines and a single purpose.
architecture.nocode: The rule in the issue template and the discipline of splitting large jobs into several issues.
architecture.code: A CI warning when a PR crosses the line threshold, as a reminder, not a blocker.
architecture.why: Human review is the main brake, and it only works with diffs a person actually reads. Five hundred lines get approved on faith; eighty get read. Diff size is the regulator of the whole system.

architecture.what: Smoke tests for critical routes plus tests for the code that changes, run on every PR before human review.
architecture.nocode: The agent writes the tests (it's one of the things it does best) against the list of critical routes you decide.
architecture.code: GitHub Actions running tests and linter on every PR; the branch doesn't merge in red.
architecture.why: Tests are the reviewer that never gets tired or rushed. With agents they serve double duty: they stop the error and they teach the agent what "working" means in your project, because it reads and runs them while it works.

architecture.what: A person reads the diff, understands what it does and why, and approves or requests changes. It's the only link with no machine.
architecture.nocode: This kit's review checklist: what to look at in an agent diff in five minutes.
architecture.code: The same, plus the agent's own pass first, summarizing its diff and flagging its doubts.
architecture.why: You approve, not the agent, and you answer to the client. Structured review (what it touches, what it could break, what I'd do differently) is where your judgment scales: it's your real job in this chain.

architecture.what: Merging to main publishes on its own, with follow-up verification: the site loads, the three critical routes respond.
architecture.nocode: Vercel connected to the repository; after every deploy, a two-minute glance at the critical routes.
architecture.code: The same plus an automated smoke test against production after deploy.
architecture.why: If deploying is costly, changes pile up and get shipped in batches, and batches break things. Small, frequent deploys are safer than big, ceremonial ones, as long as link 8 exists.

architecture.what: Going back to the previous version in two minutes, knowing how because you've done it.
architecture.nocode: Vercel's Instant Rollback, rehearsed once in cold conditions and noted in the playbook.
architecture.code: Commit revert and redeploy, plus a separate plan for changes with data migrations (the ones that don't revert with a button).
architecture.why: A rehearsed rollback turns an all-night incident into a five-minute annoyance. And it changes your deploy psychology: whoever knows how to roll back deploys without fear, and whoever deploys without fear deploys small and often.

stack.nocode: Claude Code in the project's terminal: reads the repository, runs tests, makes commits.
stack.code: Claude Code or Codex depending on preference; either way, a context file in the repository and work on a branch.
stack.pick: One, learned well, with method. Jumping from agent to agent every week is like changing employees every Monday: you lose accumulated context. This kit's method works for any of them.

stack.nocode: GitHub: templated issues, branches, PRs and main protection from the web UI.
stack.code: The same with the CLI (gh) to stay in the terminal.
stack.pick: GitHub without a doubt: agents understand it natively, branch protection is the system's structural brake, and the free plan more than covers a small team.

stack.nocode: The agent writes the tests (ask for them with every change); run them by hand before merging, at first.
stack.code: Vitest or your stack's runner, and GitHub Actions running it on every PR with the linter.
stack.pick: Start with smoke tests for the three critical routes and grow from there. Perfect coverage is the enemy of coverage that exists: three tests that always run beat a hundred planned ones.

stack.nocode: Vercel connected to the repository: a preview per PR and production on merge to main.
stack.code: The same, or Docker on a VPS if the project already lives there; the rule is identical: main deploys itself, and there's a rollback button.
stack.pick: If the project fits Vercel, it's the best brake-to-effort ratio: free PR previews and one-button rollback. Don't migrate a working project just for this.

stack.nocode: At first: Vercel's failed-deploy alert and your two-minute glance after every deploy.
stack.code: Sentry or similar once the project has real users: you find out before the client does.
stack.pick: At the minimum scope, the after-the-fact glance is enough. Set up Sentry when the cost of finding out late outweighs the half hour to configure it: the first client who tells you already crossed that line.

stack.nocode: This kit's n8n flow: a labeled issue triggers the agent's plan, you approve it, and it's all logged.
stack.code: The same with a script over GitHub webhooks if you'd rather not run n8n.
stack.pick: The circuit is optional at the minimum scope and gold at standard: it turns "stuff people asked for" into a visible queue with a plan and approval per job.

fields: How you check it's done, observably
What doesn't get touched in this job
The plan the agent proposed before working
new, plan_proposed, approved, on_branch, in_review, merged, discarded
The branch it was worked on
Who read the diff and approved
data.note: The boundaries field is what prevents the most agent errors: "don't touch authentication or the database schema" written in the job is worth more than any after-the-fact correction.

fields: yes/no: were the critical routes checked afterward
empty, or what happened and how long it took to resolve
data.note: The incident column with "how long it took" is your real rollback metric. If a month racks up incidents that don't resolve in minutes, the playbook is rusty: time for a drill.

fields: What must always work: the homepage loads, the form submits, the payment charges
The test that covers it, or a manual click while it doesn't exist yet
what happens if it fails: loses sales, loses data, annoys
data.note: This short list (three to six routes per project) is the operational definition of "working." Everything else can fail for a while; this can't. Smoke tests and the post-deploy glance come from here.

phases.title: Repository with brakes
phases.goal: Leave the project with the structural brakes in place: protected branches, an issue template, agent context, and critical routes written down.
phases.deliverable: The organized repository: protected main, job template, agent context file, and the list of critical routes with severity.
done: Nobody can push directly to main, not even you: everything goes through a PR
The issue template exists with change, boundaries and acceptance criteria
The agent context file is in the repository and tested with a question
The critical routes are written down with their severity and how they're tested today

steps.title: Run the kickoff brief with your real scares
steps.action: Fill out the kickoff prompt, especially the list of scares and the real state of the repository, without dressing it up. Answer the three questions and keep the build order.
steps.expect: Your chain with the unbraked links marked and the build order against your specific scares.
steps.stuck: If the real state embarrasses you (everything on main, zero tests), even better: an honest diagnosis is the only useful one. The kit is designed exactly to get you out of there.

steps.title: Protect main and create the job template
steps.action: Turn on main protection: require PR, and checks once you have them. Create the issue template with the three fields: what to change, what not to touch, how it's checked. Write a first real issue with it.
steps.expect: A direct push to main gets rejected (test it), and a real issue written with the template.
steps.stuck: Protection will slow you down on day one and feel like a nuisance. That's the sign it's working: the shortcut you close for yourself is the same one you close for a rushed agent.

steps.title: Write the agent's context
steps.where: The repository, with the context prompt
steps.action: Use the agent-context prompt to write the project's CLAUDE.md: what it is, how to run it, how it's tested, what not to touch, and the project's quirks a newcomer should know.
steps.expect: A one-page file at the repository root. Test: open the agent and ask how the tests are run; it should answer from the file.
steps.stuck: If you don't know the project's quirks, ask the agent: "read this repository and tell me what would surprise a new developer." Its answer is an excellent draft of the file.

steps.title: Write the critical routes with severity
steps.where: A sheet or the repository itself
steps.action: List the three to six things that must always work in each project, what happens if they fail, and how they're checked today (even a manual click). It's the kit's critical_route table.
steps.expect: A short, brutal list: "the order form submits; if it fails, we lose sales; tested by sending a fake one."
steps.stuck: If you come up with fifteen critical routes, they're not critical: rank by "would they call me today if this fails?" and cut to six. The short list is the one that actually gets checked.

steps.title: Rehearse the rollback cold
steps.action: With everything working, make a trivial change, deploy, and roll it back with Instant Rollback. Time it and write down the exact steps in the playbook.
steps.expect: You know how to get back to the previous version in under two minutes, and it's written down how.
steps.stuck: Doing it cold, with no incident, is the only stress-free time to learn it. If your deploy has no easy rollback, you've just found your number-one priority.

phases.title: The method of working with the agent
phases.goal: Close the issue → branch → small diff → tests → PR loop with the agent three times, until it comes naturally.
phases.deliverable: Three real jobs completed with the full method, and the PR review checklist refined with what you learned.
done: Three real issues have gone through the full cycle to merge
No diff exceeded ~200 lines; the ones that were going to were split into two jobs
Every change arrived with its tests, and they passed before review
You've rejected or trimmed at least one agent proposal (if not, you're not really reviewing)

steps.title: Assign the job with the job prompt
steps.where: The agent, in the project's terminal
steps.action: Take the first issue and use the assign-to-agent prompt: ask for the plan first (which files, what approach, what risks) and do NOT let it write code until you approve the plan.
steps.expect: A five-line plan you can judge: files it'll touch, approach, and what it leaves out. You say "go ahead" or correct the plan.
steps.stuck: If the plan proposes touching eight files for a small change, don't approve it: either the issue is poorly scoped or the agent is overreaching. Ask it: "what's the version of this change that touches two files?"

steps.title: Demand the small diff and the tests
steps.action: Let the agent work on the branch with the approved plan. Ask for tests for the change in the same job. When it's done, have it summarize its own diff and doubts before opening the PR.
steps.expect: A branch with the change and its tests, a diff under 200 lines, and the agent's honest summary (good ones flag their own doubts).
steps.stuck: If the diff comes out huge, don't skim it: ask it to split it ("separate the refactor from the fix into two commits" or two PRs outright). Reviewing on faith once starts the habit.

steps.title: Review the PR with the checklist
steps.action: Use this kit's PR-review prompt as a guide: what it touches, what it could break, what it does that you didn't ask for, what's missing. Approve, request changes, or reject. Note what the agent systematically does wrong: it goes into the context file.
steps.expect: A five-to-fifteen-minute review where you understand the change. And one or two new lines for CLAUDE.md ("don't use X, here we use Y").
steps.stuck: If you don't understand part of the diff, don't approve it out of embarrassment: ask the agent to explain it line by line. Explaining is free, and understanding is your one non-delegable job.

steps.title: Merge, deploy and verify
steps.action: Merge the PR, let it deploy on its own, and do the critical-routes glance. Log the row in the deploy record with verified: yes.
steps.expect: The change in production, critical routes checked, and the record up to date. Total cycle time for a small change: should fit in an afternoon.
steps.stuck: If merging scares you, that's information: what check would let you merge calmly? That check is your next smoke test.

steps.title: Repeat twice more and refine
steps.action: Complete two more jobs of different types (a bug and an improvement). After each, thirty seconds of retro: which link creaked? Adjust the template, the context, or the review checklist.
steps.expect: By the third job, the cycle comes naturally and you have a method calibrated to your project.
steps.stuck: If the agent repeats a mistake despite the context, promote it: from the general CLAUDE.md to the first line of the job. What's in the job gets followed more than what's in the file.

phases.title: CI and the job circuit
phases.goal: Have tests run themselves on every PR, and have jobs enter through a circuit with plan and approval logged.
phases.deliverable: CI running tests and linter on every PR, and this kit's flow turning labeled issues into approved plans.
done: Every PR runs tests and linter on its own, and main requires green checks
Smoke tests for the critical routes exist and run in CI
The job circuit works: labeled issue → agent plan → your approval → record
A test job has gone through the whole circuit with its trail

steps.title: Build smoke tests for the critical routes
steps.where: The agent, over your route list
steps.action: Assign the agent smoke tests for the critical-route list, one per route, with the phase-2 method (plan first, small diff). They're simple tests: the route responds, the form validates, the main flow completes.
steps.expect: One test per critical route, running locally with one command. Writing tests is one of the things an agent does best: use it.
steps.stuck: Don't chase the perfect test with mocks for everything: the smoke test checks that the big thing works. Depth later, existence first.

steps.title: Turn on CI
steps.action: Assign the agent the Actions workflow: install, lint and test on every PR. Turn it on, open a test PR and check the status. Then add the check as a required status for main protection.
steps.expect: A PR with a green check, and a PR with a test broken on purpose that can't be merged.
steps.stuck: The deliberately-broken-test check isn't optional: a CI you've never seen fail, you don't know whether it actually brakes. Break something, watch it go red, fix it.

steps.title: Import the job circuit
steps.action: Import this kit's flow, connect credentials (GitHub webhook to n8n, the model's, Sheets, Slack) and configure the repository webhook so issues reach the flow.
steps.expect: When you label an issue "agent," the flow proposes a work plan, sends it to you for approval, and publishes it as a comment on the issue once approved.
steps.stuck: If GitHub's webhook doesn't arrive, check Settings > Webhooks delivery history in the repository: it tells you the exact error. It's almost always the test URL instead of the production one.

steps.title: Run a real job through the circuit
steps.action: Write a real issue with the template, label it, approve the plan that arrives in Slack, and work the job with the agent following that plan. Close the whole cycle.
steps.expect: The issue with its plan commented, the approval logged in the sheet, and the change merged with its PR.
steps.stuck: If the plan the flow proposes is worse than what the agent would give you in the terminal, put more context into the node's prompt: the issue template and boundaries are the minimum; add the critical routes.

steps.title: Decide what's too much for the circuit
steps.action: Write the list of changes that NEVER go through the fast lane: data migrations, payments, authentication, major dependencies. For those: same issue, but plan reviewed cold, tested in preview, and shipped during quiet hours.
steps.expect: A short, clear list in the playbook of which changes require the slow path, and what the slow path consists of.
steps.stuck: The list comes from your phase-1 scares: every past scare points to a category for the slow lane. Scares are tuition already paid; use it.

phases.title: Production, incidents and delivery
phases.goal: Watch production, rehearse the incident before you have it, and leave the method written down so someone else (or you in six months) can operate it.
phases.deliverable: The incident playbook rehearsed with a drill, the month's metrics, and the complete method sheet.
done: The incident drill is done: something was broken on purpose and recovered with the playbook
The deploy record has been kept up to date for a month with its verified column
You know how much the system costs per month: agent, tools and your hours
The full playbook exists: method, critical routes, slow lane, incidents and access

steps.title: The Friday-afternoon drill
steps.action: Trigger a controlled incident: merge into main a branch with a visible but harmless error (broken text on the homepage). Detect it with your verification, and recover with the playbook: rollback, confirmation, and the real fix afterward with the normal method.
steps.expect: Incident detected and reverted in under five minutes, with the playbook steps confirmed or corrected.
steps.stuck: If you don't dare do the drill on this project, that's the drill's conclusion: your production depends on nothing ever happening. Do it on a smaller project and carry over what you learned.

steps.title: Measure the month with honest numbers
steps.action: Count the month: jobs completed, average time from issue to production, deploys with incidents, and cost (agent subscription, tokens if billed via API, tools and your hours). Use the method's cost prompt.
steps.expect: Four numbers you can compare month over month and show a client or your boss: throughput, speed, incident rate, cost.
steps.stuck: If time from issue to production is worse than before the method, look at where the wait happens: it's almost always your own review queue. The fix is dispatching reviews daily, not loosening the brakes.

steps.title: Dependency and access audit
steps.action: Run the basic security-audit prompt: secrets kept out of the code (environment variables, not files), dependencies with known vulnerabilities, GitHub and Vercel access held by two people with no ghost invites.
steps.expect: A short list of findings with fixes, and the quarterly habit noted down. Agents clone patterns from existing code: a secret in the code multiplies.
steps.stuck: If a key shows up in the Git history, rotating it is the only real cleanup: deleting it from the code doesn't delete it from the history. Rotate first, clean up after.

steps.title: Write the full playbook
steps.where: The repository (docs/) or wherever your documentation lives
steps.action: Use the playbook prompt: the method on one page, critical routes, the slow lane, the incident procedure with the drill's steps, access, and cost. It's this kit's delivery artifact.
steps.expect: A document that lets another technical person (or you with your head elsewhere) operate the system: assign, review, deploy, revert.
steps.stuck: The test: give a small job to another technical person (or do it yourself following only the playbook, with no memory). Every doubt is a missing line.

steps.title: Extend the method to the next project
steps.action: Copy the infrastructure to the next project: issue template, main protection, agent context, critical routes, and CI. With the method learned, it's an afternoon per project.
steps.expect: The second project with the brakes in place in a fraction of the first project's time. That's the method's payoff.
steps.stuck: Don't copy the CLAUDE.md as-is: every project has its own quirks. Copy the structure, rewrite the content with the agent reading the new repository.

prompts.name: Write the agent's context file
prompts.when: When setting up each project, and any time the agent repeats a mistake the file should prevent.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a technical lead documenting a project for a code agent (Claude Code, Codex) that will work on it daily. We're going to write the context file (CLAUDE.md) that will live at the repository root. It must fit on one page: the agent reads it whole every session, and every useless line dilutes the useful ones.

The project:
- What it is and for whom: [WHAT IT IS]
- Tech and main folder structure: [STACK]
- How it's run locally and how changes are tested: [COMMANDS]
- What an agent must NEVER touch without explicit permission: [UNTOUCHABLES]
- The project's quirks: odd decisions with a reason, house conventions, known traps: [QUIRKS]
- The critical routes (what can't break): [CRITICAL ROUTES]

Write the file with exactly these sections and this spirit:

1. What this is (two lines): purpose and user. The agent decides better when it knows what the code is for.
2. Commands: run, test, lint, build. Literal, copyable. If a command needs something first (env vars, services), say so on the same line.
3. Architecture in six lines: where things live, and the flow of a piece of data end to end in one sentence.
4. Working rules: small diff (one intent per branch), tests with every change, and the UNTOUCHABLES list with the reason for each in half a line ("don't touch /lib/payments: it processes real charges, changes only via the slow lane").
5. Conventions and quirks: only the ones a newcomer would unknowingly violate. With the reason: rules with a reason get respected; whims get ignored.
6. How to know nothing is broken: the verification commands and the critical routes it should check before considering anything finished.

Style rules: short, imperative sentences. No project history or long justifications. If a section of my info is thin, write [FILL IN: what's missing] instead of padding with generalities: invented context is worse than a visible gap.

fill.example: Internal order app for the distributor: sales reps order from their phone, warehouse fulfills
React + Vite, Supabase; /src/pages, /src/components, /src/lib (data client)
npm run dev; npm test; npm run lint. Needs .env with Supabase keys

fill.what: What the agent doesn't touch alone
fill.example: The database schema, /src/lib/auth.ts, and the Vercel configuration
Dates are always UTC because warehouse and reps are in different time zones; we deliberately don't use a form library
Create order, warehouse listing, and the delivery-note PDF

prompts.expect: A one-page CLAUDE.md with copyable commands, untouchables with reasons, and final verification. Tested by asking the agent something the file answers.
prompts.stuck: The quality test: open a fresh agent session and ask for a small change. If it asks something the file already says, the file doesn't say it clearly. If it touches an untouchable, section 4 needs more force.

prompts.name: Assign a change to the agent: plan first
prompts.when: At the start of every job with the agent, in the project's terminal.
prompts.prompt:
You're going to work on a job in this repository. Before writing a single line of code, I want your plan. We always work this way: short plan, my approval, and only then code.

The job (issue #[NUMBER]):
- What needs to change: [CHANGE]
- What is NOT touched in this job: [BOUNDARIES]
- Acceptance criteria (how to check it's done): [CRITERIA]

Give me the plan in this format and under fifteen lines:

1. Approach: how you'll solve it, in two or three sentences. If there are two reasonable approaches, name both, say which you choose and why in one line.
2. Files: the list of files you'll touch and what you'll do in each, one line per file. If the list exceeds five files, stop and propose how to split the job in two.
3. Tests: what tests you'll write or modify to cover the change, and how they prove the acceptance criteria.
4. Risks: what could break with this change and how you'll check it. Look at the project context's critical routes.
5. Doubts: what the job leaves unclear that you're tempted to decide on your own. I'd rather have three questions now than one surprise in the diff.

Rules for once I approve the plan:
- Work on branch [BRANCH]. Don't even think about touching main.
- Small diff: if while implementing you discover more is needed than planned, stop and tell me; don't expand scope on your own initiative.
- No opportunistic refactors: if you see improvable code outside the job, note it at the end as a suggestion, don't change it.
- Run the tests and linter before calling it done, and give me the literal result.
- When finished, summarize your diff: what you changed, why, and which part leaves you least comfortable.

If the job conflicts with the project context's UNTOUCHABLES, say so now and don't proceed.

fill.what: The change from the issue, pasted
fill.example: The order form must validate that quantity is greater than zero before submitting
Don't touch the data schema or the listing component; only the form and its validation
Submitting with quantity 0 shows an error and doesn't create the order; with 1, creates the order normally
fix/47-validate-quantity

prompts.expect: A fifteen-line plan with approach, files, tests, risks and doubts, and no code until you approve. Afterward, a small diff with passing tests and its honest summary.
prompts.stuck: If the agent jumps into coding skipping the plan, cut it off and repeat the prompt's first line. And if its "doubts" are always empty, ask explicitly: "tell me the two decisions you made on your own because the job didn't specify." There always are some.

prompts.name: Review an agent PR in fifteen minutes
prompts.when: With every open PR, before merging. It's your link: don't delegate it to whoever wrote the code.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a code reviewer experienced with changes written by AI agents. I'll give you a diff and its context, and I want a structured review that helps me decide: approve, request changes, or reject. The final call is mine; your job is making sure nothing slips past me.

Context:
- The job (issue): [ISSUE]
- The boundaries it had: [BOUNDARIES]
- The acceptance criteria: [CRITERIA]
- The project's critical routes: [ROUTES]
- The full diff: [DIFF]
- Test and linter results: [CHECKS]

Review in this order, designed for agent diffs:

1. Scope: does the diff do what the issue asks and NOTHING more? List everything the diff touches that the issue didn't ask for (renames, opportunistic refactors, new dependencies, mass formatting changes). With agents, scope creep is defect number one.
2. Boundaries: does it touch anything on the boundaries or untouchables list? If so, it's an outright rejection, say so first.
3. Criteria: does the change meet the acceptance criteria? Do the new tests prove it or just brush against it? A test that wouldn't fail if the bug came back isn't a test.
4. Breakage: what could this diff break outside itself? Look at usages of what changes, the critical routes, and edge cases (empty, null, duplicate, huge size).
5. Silent quality issues: swallowed errors that aren't logged, missing awaits, hardcoded secrets or URLs, oddly toned user-facing text, and copied code that already existed elsewhere in the project in another form.
6. Dependencies: if it adds one, was it needed? Is it maintained and well known? A new dependency is a long-term decision made inside a diff.

Output format: a table with finding, severity (blocks / request change / suggestion), and the line or file. Then your recommendation in one line with why. If the diff is clean, say so in one line and don't invent nitpicks: reviews that always find something teach the team to ignore them.

fill.example: Validate quantity > 0 on the order form
Neither the data schema nor the listing component
Quantity 0 shows a visible error; a valid quantity creates the order
Create order, warehouse listing, delivery-note PDF
git diff main...fix/47-validate-quantity (or the diff from the Files changed tab)
12 tests green, linter clean

prompts.expect: A findings table with severity and location, and the reasoned recommendation. Scope creep and violated boundaries flagged first.
prompts.stuck: This assisted review doesn't replace your reading: use it as a second pass, not the only one. If it consistently finds things you missed, your first pass needs more calm, not more tooling.

prompts.name: Calculate the system's real monthly cost
prompts.when: At the close of every month, and before quoting maintenance to a client.
prompts.prompt:
Help me calculate the real monthly cost of my code-agent maintenance system, and compare it to what it used to cost. I want figures I can redo and defend, not a feeling of productivity.

Month's data:
- Jobs completed, by type (bug, improvement, task): [JOBS]
- Agent subscription or usage: monthly plan, or tokens if billed via API: [AGENT]
- Other paid tools in the system (extra CI, monitoring, n8n): [TOOLS]
- My hours in the system, broken out: writing issues, reviewing PRs, deploying and verifying, incidents: [HOURS]
- What my hour (or whoever does it) is worth: [HOURLY RATE]
- How it used to be: how long a small change used to take on average, from request to production, and how many a month: [BEFORE]

Give me, in this order:

1. The month's total cost broken down: agent + tools + hours. Hours are almost always the big line: put them first, in euros.
2. Cost per completed job, and which jobs drive it up (the ones going down the slow lane cost more, and that's fine: separate them).
3. An honest comparison with before: jobs per month before and now, average time before and now, and where it hasn't improved. If the "before" figure is from memory, mark it as an estimate.
4. The break-even point: how many jobs a month make the system pay for its fixed costs, so you know whether a small project justifies it.
5. The three levers that would cut cost most, each in euros: almost always daily batch reviews (less context-switching), better issues (less back-and-forth with the agent), and moving trivial jobs to a cheaper model.
6. If this is for billing a client's maintenance: the monthly rate that covers N jobs with margin, and what happens with job N+1.

For per-token API pricing: if you're not sure of the current figure, write CHECK THE OFFICIAL WEBSITE and leave the formula with the gap. Don't invent prices.

fill.what: What was completed in the month
fill.example: 14 jobs: 6 bugs, 6 small improvements, 2 via the slow lane
€90/month subscription, no separate API
Everything on free plans; self-hosted n8n on a €6 VPS

fill.what: Your hours broken down by activity
fill.example: Issues 2h, reviews 6h, deploys and verification 2h, incidents 1h
Before: about 6 changes a month, each 2-4 days from request to production

prompts.expect: The breakdown with hours in euros first, cost per job, an honest comparison with its estimates marked, the break-even point, and the levers in euros.
prompts.stuck: If the result says the system doesn't pay off, before dismantling it, look at where the hours go: a review queue cleared once a week inflates everything. Do daily twenty-minute reviews and recalculate.

prompts.name: Basic repository security audit
prompts.when: When setting up the system, and every quarter after.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a pragmatic security auditor for small projects maintained with code agents. I'm not after a pentest: I want the short list of holes that really bite projects like mine, with how to check each and how to fix it. One important nuance: code agents copy the patterns they see in the repository, so an existing bad pattern multiplies on its own.

My project:
- What it is and what data it handles: [PROJECT]
- Stack and where it's deployed: [STACK]
- How secrets (keys, tokens) are managed today: [SECRETS]
- Who has access to GitHub, the deploy, and the database: [ACCESS]
- Dependencies: when they were last updated and how: [DEPENDENCIES]
- What an agent wrote in recent months: [AGENT PARTS]

Give me the audit in this order:

1. Secrets: where to look for forgotten keys in my case (code, Git history, uploaded config files, CI logs, exported n8n flows), the command or click to check each, and the rule: if one turns up, rotate it that day, because deleting it from the code doesn't delete it from the history.
2. Access: the review of who can do what in GitHub, deployment, and the database. The three typical failures: the collaborator who's no longer around, a personal token used as if it were the organization's, and everyone with admin permissions.
3. Dependencies: how to list the vulnerable ones in my specific stack (command included), the criteria for what to fix now versus what can wait, and why major upgrades go via the slow lane.
4. The dangerous patterns an agent would clone: unvalidated input, concatenated SQL, swallowed errors, open CORS, permissions checked only in the UI. Tell me how to search for each in my code and, if found, how to fix the pattern AND add the rule to the agent's context file so it doesn't repeat it.
5. Deployment: basic headers, environment variables properly separated per environment, and the database not accepting connections from the whole world.
6. The quarterly routine: the five points above in a twenty-minute version, so it actually happens.

For every possible finding: severity for MY case (based on the data I handle), not in the abstract. A project with no personal data and one with payments don't share the same priority list.

fill.what: What it is and what data it touches
fill.example: Internal order app; customer names and prices, no payments or sensitive data
React + Supabase, deployed on Vercel
Environment variables in Vercel; I suspect there's an old key in the history
Me on everything; the previous developer might still be a collaborator
Not updated in a year; npm audit never run
The last three months of changes: forms, validations, and the delivery-note PDF

prompts.expect: A checklist with command or click, severity for your case, fixes, the new rules for the agent's context, and the twenty-minute quarterly routine.
prompts.stuck: Run the checks for real and write down the result, even if it's "clean." An audit that's read but not run gives the worst kind of feeling: the feeling of security.

prompts.name: Write the system's playbook
prompts.when: At the end of setup, and updated after every incident or change of method.
prompts.prompt:
Write the operations playbook for a code-agent software maintenance system, for a technical person who didn't build it (or for me in six months, which is the same thing). Three pages max. It must allow the full system to be operated: assign, review, deploy, revert, and respond to an incident.

System data:
- Projects covered and where each lives: [PROJECTS]
- The job method: issue template, approval circuit if any: [METHOD]
- The agent and its context: [AGENT]
- CI and tests: what runs and where: [CI]
- Deploy and rollback per project: [DEPLOY]
- The slow lane: which changes require it and what it involves: [SLOW LANE]
- Critical routes per project: [ROUTES]
- Access and secrets: who has what and where it's stored: [ACCESS]
- Record-keeping: where jobs and deploys are logged: [RECORD]

The playbook has these sections and no others:

1. The system in ten lines: the full chain with the reason for each brake in half a line. Whoever reads it should understand what each piece protects before skipping it.
2. Operating a normal job, step by step with commands: from issue to production, including the plan prompt to the agent, review with its checklist, and post-deploy verification.
3. The slow lane: the exact list of changes that require it and its extra steps. In bold: when in doubt, slow lane.
4. Production incident: the rollback steps per project, timed in the drill, in a follow-along format. Revert first, investigate after. Include how to confirm the revert worked (the critical routes) and where to log the incident.
5. The five most likely problems in a table: symptom, cause, action, and when to escalate (and to whom).
6. What is never done, with the reason: merging without review "because it's small," deploying without verifying, giving the agent access to the untouchables, turning off CI "temporarily."
7. System maintenance: the monthly routine (metrics, record kept up to date) and the quarterly one (security audit, drill if it's been over six months since the last).
8. Access: what's needed to operate, where the keys are (the vault, not the keys themselves), and the two-person rule.

Style: imperative, literal commands, zero filler. If any data I gave you is incomplete, leave [FILL IN: what] visible in its place.

fill.example: company-website (Vercel), order-app (Vercel + Supabase)
Templated issue; the 'agent' label triggers the plan via n8n; I approve in Slack
Claude Code; CLAUDE.md at every root, updated after every repeated mistake
GitHub Actions: lint + tests on every PR; main requires green checks

fill.what: How each project publishes and rolls back
fill.example: Merging to main deploys on Vercel; rollback with Instant Rollback (rehearsed: 90 seconds)

fill.what: The changes with a special path
fill.example: Data migrations, authentication, major dependencies: cold plan + preview + quiet hours
website: home and contact form; app: create order, listing, PDF
GitHub and Vercel: me and the manager; keys in the company's vault
'Maintenance' sheet: jobs and deploys tabs

prompts.expect: Three operable pages: the chain with reasons, the job step-by-step, the slow lane, the timed incident, the problem table, and the routines.
prompts.stuck: The playbook's test is the phase-4 drill run by someone else (or by you with no memory, following only the paper). Whichever step you hesitate on is the poorly written step.

Approved, it's published as a comment on the issue so you can work with the agent on that plan; rejected, it's logged with its reason. The flow doesn't write code or touch the repository beyond the comment: it prepares and organizes, the code is worked in the terminal with the kit's method.

costs.free: There are limited entry tiers; for daily production work, plan to pay.
costs.paid: Monthly subscription or API usage depending on tool and use. CHECK THE OFFICIAL WEBSITE: plans change often.
costs.note: It's the expense that pays off most once the method is in place: the same agent with vague issues and no brakes produces rework that eats the savings.

costs.free: The free plan covers private repos, PRs, branch protection, and plenty of Actions minutes for a small team.
costs.paid: Paid for larger teams or heavy CI. CHECK THE OFFICIAL WEBSITE.
costs.note: Watch your Actions minutes if your tests are slow: a 20-minute test suite on every PR burns through the month fast. Fast smoke tests first.

costs.free: Vercel free for personal and small projects; a basic VPS €5-10/month.
costs.paid: Vercel paid for serious commercial use. CHECK THE OFFICIAL WEBSITE for terms.
costs.note: The real cost of deployment isn't hosting: it's the incident with no rollback. The two minutes of the drill are worth more than any pricing optimization.

costs.free: Self-hosted n8n and Sheets, €0. The circuit uses one AI call per job: pennies.
costs.paid: Cloud n8n by executions. CHECK THE OFFICIAL WEBSITE.
costs.note: It's the cheapest piece of the system and the one that gives you traceability. Don't cut it to save money: cut anything else first.

costs.free: Never zero: writing issues, reviewing PRs, verifying deploys, and the monthly ritual.
costs.paid: With the method running smoothly, 8-12 hours a month for a couple of active projects. Multiply by your rate.
costs.note: The big line item, and the one the method optimizes: every hour of good review saves the three hours of firefighting it would have caused.

legal: Responsibility for the code: you answer to your client whether the agent wrote it or not. The maintenance contract shouldn't mention "the AI did it" as an excuse or a defense: this kit's human review is your due diligence.

Intellectual property of generated code: review your agent tool's terms on ownership and use of the code it produces. For client work, have the contract state that delivered code belongs to the client, and that you can guarantee that with your tool.

Dependency licenses: every package the agent adds carries its own license. Copyleft ones (GPL and family) in a client's proprietary product are a serious problem: PR review includes checking which dependencies come in and under what license.

Third-party code in the repository: if you maintain a legacy project, confirm what you can reuse and modify. A repository with no clear license from a departed previous developer is a conversation with the client, not a detail.
Personal data in development: don't use real production data for testing or pass it to the agent in prompts. Fictitious data for dev and tests; if you need realistic volume, generate synthetic data.

Confidentiality with clients: the client's code travels to the agent provider. Check that your contract with the client allows it (or get explicit permission), and that the provider's terms on not training with your data are noted with a date.

Production access: the agent doesn't need production credentials to write code, so it doesn't have any. Production environment variables live only in the deploy dashboard, never in files the agent reads or the repository stores.
Change log as evidence: Git history, reviewed PRs, and the deploy record are your evidence of diligent work for a client or an auditor. Protect that trail: it's part of your billable value.

If the software handles personal data (forms, users), changes touching those flows also go via the slow lane for GDPR: a change that logs excess data or exposes it is a legal incident, not just a technical one.
This is practical guidance, not legal advice. Maintenance contracts, questionable licenses, or data incidents: bring in a licensed professional.

risks.risk: The agent rewrites half the project for one job
risks.sign: A thousand-line diff to "fix a button"; files touched that nobody asked for
risks.fix: Plan before code, boundaries in the issue, and the small-diff rule with the discipline to split. If it already happened: don't review on faith, throw away the branch and reassign in two issues.

risks.sign: Two-minute approvals of 400-line diffs; "it looked fine" as the justification
risks.fix: Small diffs (the root cause), the review checklist, and your own rule of never approving what you can't explain in two sentences.

risks.risk: A change breaks production and there's no fast rollback
risks.sign: The afternoon incident lasts into the night; it gets patched "forward" with live fixes
risks.fix: The rollback rehearsed cold and the playbook with the steps. Revert first, investigate after: the reverse order is what stretches the nights.

risks.risk: Tests exist but don't actually stop anything
risks.sign: PRs merged with red checks "because it was urgent"; tests disabled for months
risks.fix: Main protection requiring checks, and periodically testing the deliberately-broken test. A brake you can skip in a hurry isn't a brake.

risks.risk: The agent learns the bad patterns already in the repository
risks.sign: Every new change repeats the same flaw (swallowed errors, concatenated SQL) that already existed
risks.fix: The quarterly audit catches the pattern, it gets fixed once, and the rule goes into the context file. The agent amplifies what it sees: give it something good to see.

risks.risk: Critical changes going through the fast lane
risks.sign: A data migration merged on a Friday as if it were a text change
risks.fix: The slow-lane list written in the playbook and in the context's untouchables, with the circuit flagging it in the plan. When in doubt, slow lane.

risks.sign: Nobody else knows how to deploy, roll back, or where the keys are
risks.fix: The playbook tested by someone else and the two-person rule on access. If there's no other technical person, the detailed playbook is your life insurance (and your vacation).

risks.risk: The agent's subscription or API bill spikes
risks.sign: The month's invoice triples the previous one with no more jobs
risks.fix: The monthly cost-per-job record, and hunt for the pattern: it's almost always a poorly scoped job that produced twenty iterations. The fix is the issue, not the model.

pricing.note: Close the scope: one project, up to N critical routes with tests, and the playbook. The maintenance jobs themselves are the next contract, not this one.

pricing.what: Changes that don't fit maintenance: migrations, new modules, integrations. Quoted per job with its plan up front.

pricing.tier: Training: the method for their team

pricing.note: For clients with their own developer. You sell them the method and keep the quarterly audit role: better business than competing with their payroll.

defend.question: Is the code written by an AI? What if it introduces a bug?
defend.answer: An agent writes it and a person signs off on it, with four brakes in between: the job defines what it can and can't touch, tests pass before anyone looks, a person reads the whole diff before approving (and diffs are small precisely so that reading is real), and the deploy has a rehearsed two-minute rollback. It will introduce bugs, like any developer: the right question is how long they live and how much damage they do, and that's what the record's metrics show.

defend.question: Why isn't this faster, if the AI programs in seconds?
defend.answer: Writing the code is the fast part, and always was. What takes time is what prevents scares: scoping the job, reviewing the diff, testing, and verifying the deploy. A small change goes from issue to production in [n] hours on average, which is in the record; what we don't do is skip review to save twenty minutes and risk an afternoon of incident.

defend.question: What happens if this breaks the website on a Friday?
defend.answer: We go back to the previous version in two minutes with a rehearsed procedure (not theoretical: we ran a drill, it's timed and written down). Revert first, investigate calmly after. And change categories that could do real damage (data, payments, access) don't even go through the fast lane: they have a slow procedure with prior testing and quiet hours.

defend.question: Does our code end up in the AI provider's hands?
defend.answer: The code travels to the agent's provider to be worked on, just as it would to an external developer. It's covered: the contract addresses it, the provider's terms on not training with client data are reviewed and dated, and production credentials are seen by neither the agent nor the repository: they live only in the deploy dashboard.

defend.question: What happens when you're on vacation, or if you leave?
defend.answer: There's a three-page playbook another technical person can use to operate everything: assign, review, deploy, and revert. It's tested, not just written. Access belongs to the organization under the two-person rule, the code is in their GitHub, and the record shows what was done each month. My value is doing it well, not being irreplaceable.

defend.question: Wouldn't a junior developer be cheaper?
defend.answer: They're different things. This system does scoped maintenance with senior judgment (the review) and tireless hands (the agent), for €[n]/month, measurable in the record. A junior brings things this doesn't, and needs management this doesn't require. For the queue of small, constant changes, the system wins on cost and traceability; for a new product, hire. And they're not mutually exclusive: the playbook is there for that future developer to work with the same method.

words: code agent
An AI that works on your repository: reads, writes, runs tests, and makes commits. Claude Code and Codex are this kit's.
issue
The job written up on GitHub: what to change, what not to touch, and how to check it's done. In this system, the issue is the prompt.
branch
A working copy of the code where a change is made without touching what's published. The cheap way to be wrong.
diff
The exact list of lines a change adds and removes. What gets reviewed. Small gets read; big gets approved on faith.
PR (pull request)
The request to merge a branch into main, with its diff and conversation visible. The place where human review happens.
CI
Continuous integration: the tests and checks that run themselves on every PR. The reviewer that never gets tired.
smoke test
A simple test that checks the essentials work: the page loads, the form submits. Existence before depth.
deploy
Publishing a version to production. In this system it's automatic on merge to main, and therefore boring.
rollback
Going back to the previously published version. Rehearsed cold, it takes two minutes; improvised live, a whole night.
slow lane
The reinforced procedure for dangerous changes: migrations, payments, access. Cold plan, prior testing, quiet hours.
